articles.title: Where was Nvidia’s security team?
articles.title_ko: Where was Nvidia’s security team?

articles.content:
Outsiders had little reason to notice when Nvidia’s longtime chief security officer and head of product security stepped down in August. Just two and a half months later, CEO Jensen Huang himself left the company over growing questions about his extramarital relationships — starting with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore data center company that U.S. investigators suspect of funneling Nvidia chips to China, then widening to reports about two separate affairs with Nvidia employees.
At the time, David Reber, who spent four years as CSO and seven at Nvidia overall, said he was leaving for health reasons. “This wasn’t a pivot I had planned. But I know what needs to come first: family and health,” he wrote on LinkedIn in late August, disclosing that he’d been diagnosed with young-onset Parkinson’s more than two years ago.
Reber’s replacement, Saša Zdjelar, previously spent 17 years at ExxonMobil in Houston, leaving as a senior IT manager before spending one year at Salesforce and several years at the cybersecurity company ReversingLabs. Zdjelar didn’t respond to questions Thursday about the transition or what the security team knew.
Nothing public connects Reber’s or Zdjelar’s role changes to the Megaspeed matter, but it seems fair to wonder what Nvidia’s security team knew about the government’s scrutiny of Megaspeed and about Huang’s relationships, and whether anyone raised concerns. Reber didn’t respond to questions Thursday. Nvidia also has not answered our related questions.
Not all of those relationships are the business of the security team. Relationships with subordinates typically fall to HR, legal, and the board. But an affair with an executive at a company under federal investigation is a different animal. (Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing.) Security specialists say affairs can create vulnerabilities that foreign intelligence services look to exploit.
Catching that kind of exposure isn’t easy. The way intelligence services collect information, much of it through everyday conversation rather than hacking, makes it especially difficult for security teams to identify risks, according to retired senior intelligence officer Nicholas Eftimiades, who says he has trained more than 1,000 corporate security professionals.
Some people inside Nvidia clearly knew parts of the picture. Nvidia’s top lawyer was engaged with the government’s Megaspeed inquiry more than a year ago, The New York Times
reported earlier this week
. (Nvidia has said it regularly contacts officials.) Reports about Huang’s relationships with employees suggest colleagues also knew of them, even if the behavior is not expressly forbidden by Nvidia’s
code of conduct
. The Times cited five Nvidia employees who said he was involved with a vice president who reported directly to him, and Reuters, citing two people, later reported a second relationship. What’s unclear is whether any of that reached security.
Even if it had reached Nvidia’s security team, Eftimiades, who wrote
Chinese Espionage Operations and Tactics
in 2020, said a security team’s resources are often limited. For one thing, they’re often underfunded because, unlike some other cost centers, they don’t drive revenue. It’s astonishingly common for CEOs to answer a security team’s warnings with “not a nickel more than compliance,” he said.
Many companies also define security very narrowly, specialists say. In an opinion piece in
The Hill
, Don Aviv, CEO of the corporate investigations firm Interfor International, and author Jeremy Hurewitz, wrote, “Too many companies still approach security primarily as a matter of protecting facilities, preventing cyberattacks, and responding to physical threats.” The two argued that “[s]ecurity teams need to pay greater attention to insider threats, including the cultivation of executives and employees by foreign intelligence services, suspicious business relationships, conflicts of interest and attempts to obtain sensitive information through trusted personal contacts.”
Still, some of it is beyond what any team can do. Speaking generally, not about Huang, Eftimiades offered a hypothetical in which a CEO complains that he can’t do something because “I’m fighting a board who doesn’t want to do this.” That tells an intelligence asset who the obstacle is. The service then asks, “Who’s the sticking point here?” and looks for ways into that person’s email and phone.
What a rival intelligence service wants is often less technology than policy insight, including who’s pushing to change export rules and who the biggest blocker is. “Intel world tends to be like cancer,” he said. “Once it gets into the body, it looks to spread and looks to reach out.”
The playbook isn’t new, Eftimiades added, “particularly for China.”  Any executive dealing with the country “will tell you that they’ve been approached.” He said there are also “tons of diplomat stories” of U.S. diplomats walking into a hotel room to find a woman on the bed. He said what’s newer compared with Soviet era spying is the relationships these services cultivate now often last years, not weeks.
Technology can augment that human intelligence, Eftimiades said, pointing to IMSI catchers are one example. These devices mimic a cell tower so that nearby phones connect to them. A basic version can cost about $1,000 and fit in a suitcase, he said, though government-grade models cost far more.
Eftimiades says no one knows yet if these were used against Huang, whose phone was presumably hardened such that compromises could be detected, if not stopped altogether. But either way, what Nvidia’s security team knew, and whether it could have acted on it, should become clearer as the board’s independent investigation and federal inquiries proceed.
In the meantime, Eftimiades said he hopes the whole episode is “a wake-up call” for U.S. industry, which he said is mostly “clueless” about China’s tactics. “We have lost trillions [of dollars] in intellectual property,” is his guess. “Whatever we think we’re doing isn’t working.”

articles.content:
Last month, chatbot platform Character.ai
filed for bankruptcy
just five years after launching. More recently, privacy-focused AI assistant Ollie
announced
its shutdown a few weeks ago.
Aside from Character.ai and Ollie, plenty of AI bets never even survive inside the companies that build them. According to
S&P Global Market Intelligence
, about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned by their corporate parents. The reasons vary: insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling, or just weak user demand.
The result is a growing AI graveyard. Below is a look at some of the most notable AI products, startups, launches, and bets that have shut down, pivoted, or significantly missed expectations. Think of it less as a scorecard of flops than as a record of what these attempts can (hopefully) teach the rest of the industry.
OpenAI has taken several stumbles
Image Credits:
SeongJoon Cho/Bloomberg / Getty Images
Even the biggest players aren’t immune. OpenAI, one of the most valuable private companies in the world, has had its own share of casualties and missteps. One of the more recent examples was its attempt to turn ChatGPT into a broader “
super app
.” On July 9, OpenAI
updated
the app to combine several experiences, including separate “Chat,” “Codex,” and “Work” modes, while renaming the traditional, familiar version “ChatGPT Classic.”
The redesign quickly drew
criticism
from users who found the new interface confusing and cluttered, and OpenAI rolled back the change
soon after
, bringing the familiar ChatGPT interface back.
That wasn’t OpenAI’s only attempt to pull everything under one roof. The company has also shut down several stand-alone apps and folded their features directly into ChatGPT — a strategy that’s worked out better than the redesign did. ChatGPT Atlas, a stand-alone AI-powered web browser, lasted less than a year before being discontinued on August 9, with its most useful features absorbed into ChatGPT.
The company did the same thing with
Operator
, an AI agent that could browse the web and complete tasks on a user’s behalf, and OpenAI has increasingly built image generation directly into ChatGPT, shrinking the role of
DALL-E
as its own separate destination for creating images.
We also can’t forget its video-sharing platform,
Sora
, which struggled with high operating costs and user-retention challenges and shut down in March 2026.
Apple’s Siri AI
Image Credits:
Artur Widak/NurPhoto / Getty Images
When Apple
unveiled
Apple Intelligence in 2024, an improved Siri was one of the highlighted features. The pitch promised a Siri that could understand context, know what was happening across apps, and get tasks done effectively.
However, Apple repeatedly
pushed back
the release of the new Siri, citing various reasons like
engineering issues and bugs
. This delay eventually contributed to a
$250 million settlement
over claims regarding how Apple marketed the AI capabilities of the iPhone 16.
Siri AI finally appeared in the
iOS 27 beta
this past July, with the new AI-powered version rolling out to English-language users first this month; support for other languages is expected to follow.
Character.ai
Image Credits:
Character.AI
Founded in 2021 by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, Character.ai was a consumer AI app that let people chat with customizable bots, many of them modeled on celebrities and fictional characters. It raised $150 million at a $1 billion valuation in 2023. Then, the next year, Google paid a reported $2.7 billion to license its technology and bring its founders back into its orbit, leaving the startup to carry on without them.
Character.ai has run into a lot of trouble over the years. Families have sued, alleging the chatbots contributed to teen suicides and self-harm, and Disney sent a cease-and-desist letter over unauthorized use of its characters. Character.ai
barred under-18 users
from open-ended chats late last year and agreed to settle several of the suits, along with Google, in early 2026.
But it wasn’t enough. The company
filed for bankruptcy
in early October, citing legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds. In an ironic twist, Disney is now the opening bidder, offering $20 million for a license to some of its intellectual property. The app is still running during the process, and the sale is expected to wrap up by late November or early December.
Relay
Relay, an AI-powered workflow automation tool built as an alternative to Zapier,
shut down
entirely in August 2026.
The product let users automate email and task workflows using AI agents, but as OpenAI, Google, and other larger platforms built similar automation directly into their own tools, five-year-old Relay struggled to hold on to a reason to exist as a stand-alone product.
Ollie
Image Credits:
Ollie
Ollie
launched in June 2026 as one of the first mainstream apps to achieve SOC 2, a privacy compliance standard.
Similar to the other family-focused agents, the idea behind
Ollie
was that families already have the information they need, but it lives across school messages, calendars, task lists, and group chats. Ollie aimed to bring those pieces together and keep them in sync. It kept track of calendars, emails, reminders, tasks, and other household details, then delivered relevant information to users through text.
However, the app faced a very common challenge: keeping up with heavyweights like Muse and Instinct. Co-founder and CEO Bill Lennon revealed the app would shut down on November 6, citing difficulties like being unable to stand out, failing to grow, and not raising enough capital.
Microsoft’s Recall
Announced at its 2024 Build developer conference, Microsoft’s
Recall feature
was pitched as an AI-powered “photographic memory” for Windows PCs, periodically taking screenshots of what a user was doing so they could later search back through their own digital history.
Predictably, the announcement triggered an immediate
backlash
over privacy and security. Critics argued that Recall could create a searchable archive of highly sensitive information, including passwords, private messages, financial details, and other activity. Microsoft delayed the feature for nearly a year, giving the company time to rethink its security and privacy protections.
Even after a redesign, the controversy hasn’t gone away. A cybersecurity researcher recently built a tool that could
extract and display data
that Recall had captured, reviving questions about whether Microsoft has actually fixed the underlying problem.
Notion Mail
Image Credits:
Notion
Notion Mail
launched in April 2025 as an AI-focused email product designed to help users organize and automate their inboxes. However, the company noticed its users were using separate AI agents to handle their email inboxes instead. As a result, Notion Mail is scheduled to shut down on
September 22
.
Humane AI Pin
Image Credits:
Brian Heater
The
Humane AI Pin
is probably one of the most well-known failures in AI hardware. Designed to provide AI features through a wearable device rather than a traditional smartphone, Humane raised $230 million from investors and garnered significant attention.
But the product struggled mightily with performance, and the situation worsened when Humane
warned
customers to stop using its charging case because of a potential battery fire risk. Humane then shut down its AI Pin business in February 2025, with most of the company’s assets
acquired by HP
for $116 million.
Rabbit R1
Image Credits:
Rabbit
The
Rabbit R1
was another heavily hyped AI device. Unveiled at CES in January 2024, the AI companion was designed to perform tasks on behalf of its owner. Rabbit said it had sold 100,000 units shortly after launch.
However, strong initial sales didn’t mean it was a strong product.
Early reviews
described the device as unfinished, with unreliable performance and a limited number of useful integrations.
The company hasn’t given up, though. It has continued
updating
the R1, positioning it as a computer controller capable of performing agentic tasks. It also recently announced a new hardware project, dubbed “Project Cyberdeck,” aimed at creating a portable device built for vibe-coding.
Huxe
Image Credits:
Huxe
Huxe
was an AI audio app, built by former developers of Google’s NotebookLM, that turned written information into conversational, podcast-style audio.
The company
shut down
in May 2026, partly as larger platforms began offering similar experiences to large existing audiences. For instance,
Spotify
has been expanding its own AI-powered audio tools.
Yupp
Image Credits:
Yupp
Yupp
was an interesting AI product: a free playground that allowed users to compare responses from hundreds of AI models side by side. Users could also vote on responses and earn cryptocurrency through the platform.
At its peak, the platform let users test more than 800 models, including from companies such as OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. But according to its founders, Yupp never achieved strong enough product-market fit to survive. The platform
shut down
in March 2026.
Figgs AI
Figgs AI operated from 2023 to 2024, letting users create and interact with customizable AI characters for role-play and storytelling. The platform reportedly drew more than 1 million users, but its developers said keeping the service free became too expensive to sustain, and they
shut it down
.

articles.content:
Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia has drawn a range of responses across Asia, with some governments moving to confirm chip supply commitments, while others are monitoring the impact on local projects or addressing ongoing investigations.
On Sunday, November 8,
Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation
after reports that Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation; Huang admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed.
Nvidia’s influence extends far beyond the United States. The chip giant has built close ties with companies worldwide, particularly in Asia, where many of its key partners play important roles in the global AI industry.
China
China’s foreign ministry
rejected allegations on November 10 that a Chinese businesswoman linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a spy, calling them groundless and a smear against Beijing.
On Friday
, a spokesperson reiterated opposition to export controls that disrupt global supply chains and stated the ministry was not aware of reports linking restricted Nvidia chips to a Shanghai data center associated with Alice Huang.
Huang’s exit has also raised uncertainty over
more than $3 billion in Chinese AI computing
projects reliant on Nvidia’s restricted processors, according to Reuters. Many of these chips are subject to U.S. export controls, making them difficult for Chinese companies to obtain.
Singapore
In Singapore, authorities seized the passport of Alice Huang, former CEO of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, in June 2025 as part of an investigation into possible false declarations regarding server purchases, according to the
Ministry of Home Affairs.
The Singapore ministry said police took her passport to ensure she remained available for questioning, as she was not based in Singapore.
The investigation
examined whether servers shipped from Singapore to Malaysia were later sent to other countries without proper declaration.
In February 2026,
police found insufficient evidence
to establish that Alice Huang had committed offenses related to the suspected false declarations, according to the ministry. However, authorities said she had knowingly provided inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed. She was issued a warning and barred from re-entering Singapore. Her passport was returned that month. Singapore
also said it received limited assistance
from U.S. authorities despite repeated requests for information about U.S. server maker Supermicro. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said its investigation into Megaspeed and six other individuals remains ongoing.  The ministry did
not identify the six individuals or
specify their alleged roles in the case.
South Korea
South Korea has close ties to Nvidia, with major chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix playing important roles in supplying memory chips used in its AI processors. Following Huang’s exit, South Korea’s Science Ministry said Nvidia had reaffirmed its plan to supply 260,000 advanced GPUs to the country and to continue joint AI projects.  Apart from that, South Korea’s government AI strategy council held an emergency meeting on Friday to assess the potential impact of Huang’s departure on the country’s AI industry, per
a local media report.
Taiwan
Taiwan’s Economy Minister Kung Ming-shin said Huang’s departure was unlikely to significantly change the growth of the global AI industry,
according to local media
. Meanwhile, Taipei’s city government
said
Nvidia’s planned overseas headquarters in the city remained on track despite the leadership change. The company has met its contractual obligations so far, and officials said they would continue to support the project.
Japan
In Japan, the Industry Ministry said the government would closely monitor Nvidia following Huang’s resignation, describing the chipmaker as an important player in Japan’s AI semiconductor industry, Reuters reported.
Deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki
said it was too early to assess the impact on the global AI industry, while stressing Japan’s commitment to ensuring a stable supply of semiconductors.

The OpenAI board member who fired Sam Altman says we still can’t trust AI CEOs
CSET’s Helen Toner says ‘we’re screwed’ if our AI safety plan rests on any one person being trusted to get this right.
by
Nilay Patel
Nov 14, 2026, 3:00 PM UTC
Link
Share
Nilay Patel
is editor-in-chief of The Verge, host of the
Decoder podcast
, and co-host of
The Vergecast
.
Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. This episode is part two of our series on AI in real life.
Helen is a well-known figure in the AI safety and policy community, though she is perhaps best known for having served on the board of OpenAI, when she was one of four board members who
voted to fire Sam Altman
. That incident, now sometimes
referred to as “the blip,”
ended with Sam coming back as CEO, Helen resigning, and a new board of directors. OpenAI has since
restructured entirely
.
But it’s worth remembering what Helen and the board were supposed to do: OpenAI’s nonprofit board existed specifically to make sure the company didn’t betray its mission to build safe AI by prioritizing profit and growth over safety. When the board actually tried to pull the lever, that accountability mechanism broke, and here we are.
Verge
subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free
Decoder
wherever you get your podcasts. Head
here
. Not a subscriber? You can
sign up here
.
Now, the
question of AI safety is everywhere
. This summer, AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic broke out of their testing environments and hacked real companies. The CEOs of these frontier labs have since called for a slowdown and asked Washington for help, but the White House’s answer was a
voluntary accord
— one that relies in part on the kind of board accountability that failed at OpenAI. Anthropic is also about to go public, which will put a whole new set of market pressures on OpenAI’s biggest competitor.
Helen has seen up close what happens when safety commitments run headlong into commercial incentives. And as she put it to me, if our hopes for the future depend on any one person being trustworthy, we’re in big trouble.
So we talked about what we might do instead: what the labs are actually trying to build, whether AI alignment is a problem that
can
be solved, and what a smarter approach to AI regulation might look like. That includes how to think about China, which is the issue that looms large in every policy conversation about AI right now — especially now
after the Jensen Huang affair
. Just for clarity, Helen and I talked before Nvidia opened its investigation and Jensen ultimately resigned, so you won’t hear us talk about that directly.
Before we get going, do me a favor and
subscribe to
Decoder
on YouTube
, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.
Okay: Helen Toner, the executive director of CSET, on the future of AI safety. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Helen Toner, you’re the executive director for the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. Welcome to
Decoder
.
Thanks so much. Great to be here.
I have wanted to talk to you for 10 million years. I am so excited you’re here. You’ve been involved in a lot of AI safety and ethics ideas for a long time. You were obviously on the board of OpenAI during what everyone has come to call “the blip.”
Now, you’re talking a lot about AI safety, about which I have 10 million questions. But let’s just start at the start. You run the Center for Security and Emerging Technology, people call it CSET. What is CSET?
It’s awesome to be here. I’m really excited to talk to you as well. CSET is a team inside Georgetown, but we’re really not academics. We’re about 50 people and have been going since 2019.
Basically in 2019, a group of us decided that there was a lot happening and a lot of emerging technologies that were becoming very relevant in the national security space, and the security space more broadly,. And some policymakers who had very important jobs did not have the time or the expertise to get across what was going on with those emerging technologies. Already at the top of our list in 2019 was AI.
Basically our mission is to do analysis that is really rigorous, but also actionable, for policymakers and analysis that is both grounded in the technology and grounded in real national security expertise and understanding and issues. We produce long reports. We go do short briefings on those long reports to busy policymakers. We have a big data team that helps us do our research. We do all kinds of cool stuff.
Can I just ask about the dynamics of that for one minute? You and I are talking the day after the midterm elections in the United States of America, and there was a big blue wave. There’s a lot of polling that says the number one issue is corruption. We’re going to throw the bums out. We’re going to start over and get rid of these corrupt guys.
The AI industry, and the tech industry, has flooded a bunch of money into politics. And then somewhere next to that is, “Oh, there’s a bunch of well-meaning researchers who are going to show up and tell you how it actually works and what the real risks are.”
It just occurs to me that maybe people don’t believe that’s effective anymore, that the money and the corruption and the AI CEO standing next to Trump have completely outweighed the well-meaning, sincere, “here are the actual problems” research that you do. What is that dynamic actually like?
It’s a reasonable concern to have, and there are definitely some spaces where money just absolutely overwhelms everything. I’m Australian. I didn’t grow up in the US, and so the amount of money in US elections is pretty mind-blowing to me, but there are limits to what money can do.
AI is a great example. In this election, there were just unbelievable amounts of money being thrown at candidates, at messages, at opposition research. There was all kinds of astroturfing on Twitter, and some very strange things trying to get anyone who talked about AI governance, regulation, safety, any of those words thrown out or not elected. It turns out to have really not worked very well.

What we see in our work is that there is a real thirst among policymakers for high-quality information. That’s members of Congress for sure, but they’re also in the executive branch, just a lot of people who have these very busy jobs and are seeing AI playing a larger and larger role in their work and their world.
In DC, if you live and work here, you know that lobbyists in DC are not just people who go in and push their company’s position, though they do do that. They’re also educators. A big reason that congressional staff and others want to have lobbyists come talk to them is because they’ll really help them understand the weeds of a given piece of legislation — what does it mean for that industry and so on and so forth.
What we find over and over again is we can go in and say, “Hey, we are independent. We’re nonpartisan. We do really rigorous work. We’re just here to help and we can go into the weeds with you as well.” There’s a ton of interest in that and appetite for that. It’s been really encouraging over the past seven to eight years.
Are you doing that with the principals, the members of Congress, or are you doing that with the staff?
Everyone and anyone. Again, we do a good amount of work with Congress on Capitol Hill, with some members of Congress, with lots of staff. We do hearings and briefings. Also, we do lots in the executive branch, with different agencies — the White House, Department of War, Department of State, Department of Commerce, all across the board at different levels, depending on the topic and what’s happening at any given moment.
The reason I’m starting here is I want to have a pretty heady conversation with you, but I know what our audience thinks and it’s just that the government doesn’t get it. There’s no way the government will ever catch up to the tech industry. There’s no way they’ll ever write a regulation. They should just get out of the way.
In this election cycle, I’ve seen a number of candidate forum videos where someone was like, “I’ve tried Claude once.” There’s some huge gap, real or perceived. I’m just trying to understand how you see that gap, how big you think that gap is, because as we get into AI safety and regulation, it’s that gap that has to close.
There absolutely is a gap. It absolutely is a big gap. It also is possible to overestimate the gap from outside, or if you’re just looking across from California. I lived in the Bay Area for three years, so I definitely am very familiar with this perspective.
I know a lot of people from the tech industry who come over and start talking to congressional staff or staffers in executive branch offices. Once they actually start having those conversations, they’re like, “Wow, these people are really smart. The staff do actually know what they’re talking about.”
With principals, it is a different issue. Some of them are in the older generations, but they’re also getting smart. It takes time and it takes effort, and these people have so many demands on their time. The cynical thing to say is they’re just busy trying to get elected, but a lot of people in these roles also just have really big other topics that they have to be thinking about. They have to be thinking about wars and healthcare and cost of living and they’re looking at a lot of other stuff from day to day.
I saw after ChatGPT, there was a wave in 2023 of, “Oh, maybe Congress is going to get activated on AI, maybe they’re going to actually do something.” It didn’t really turn into anything actually happening, but it did turn into a real moment where a lot of members of Congress and other policymakers started to get smart on AI. It takes some time to learn what a language model is. What even is AI? What is machine learning?

I definitely don’t want to say there’s no gap or the government is super smart on AI across the board, but there are some champions who are really smart. I think the staff are generally smarter than people give them credit for.

Tech
AI
Report
Jensen Huang and the decline of the visionary showman founder CEO
The Steve Jobs of GPUs has been shown the door.﻿
by
Sean Hollister
Nov 14, 2026, 12:00 PM UTC
Link
Share
Gift
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at CES 2025 in Las Vegas, Nevada, on January 6, 2025.
|  Photo by Artur Widak/NurPhoto via Getty Images
Part Of
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned. What happens next?
see all updates
Sean Hollister
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.
On January 6th, 2025, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang got his rockstar moment at last. He strode triumphantly onstage, hand raised in the air, to the claps and cheers of
a 14,000-person arena absolutely packed
with influencers and fans, their faces awash in blue glow, as he made his entrance in a black leather jacket that shimmered in the stadium’s lights.
Few are cheering for Jensen Huang now.
He has left Nvidia
after seemingly enabling
two chip smuggling scandals
and allegedly having
three extramarital affairs
, including one with an alleged Chinese spy at the same time he was mingling with President Donald Trump.
The world is watching to see
if this scandal might disrupt the entire US AI industry
and perhaps destabilize the stock market along with it. That’s because Huang wasn’t merely running
the first $5 trillion company
, he was
the
visionary leader in control of the must-have GPUs powering the worldwide AI boom, part of a company that represents around 6 percent of the S&P 500 stock market index all by itself. And he didn’t plan for succession if he ever stepped down.
The 63-year-old once said
he preferred to die on the job
; he once suggested he’d work
until he was 90 or 100
, then carry on leading the company as a robot.
It’s not easy to replace Huang, partly because he had no deputies.
Around 60 employees reported directly to the CEO
. “He built the company around himself, and everything that happened there flowed through him,” says IDC analyst and former computing journalist Tom Mainelli.
“Jensen is Nvidia, and Nvidia is Jensen,” Jon Peddie, a computer industry analyst who’s been tracking Nvidia since its inception, tells me.
But Nvidia isn’t Jensen anymore. He has left the company he cofounded 33 years ago. It’s the end of an era, and not just for Nvidia — because Jensen Huang was Big Tech’s last true example of a visionary showman founder CEO.
“He was both the visionary and the tactical leader, the closest thing tech has had to Steve Jobs,” Moor Insights & Strategy chief analyst Pat Moorhead tells me.
Elon Musk
didn’t exactly found Tesla
and has quite the track record of broken promises, and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg has
proven to be neither visionary nor showman
so far. Google’s Larry Page and Sergey Brin stepped away in 2019 as their company
dealt with growing employee turmoil
, leaving the company in the hands of Sundar Pichai, and both Microsoft and Apple have each passed the torch twice since the days of Bill Gates and Steve Jobs.
Some say Apple’s Steve Jobs broke the CEO mold, but he created a mold of his own. Huang was one of countless tech leaders who followed his example by introducing their products in keynote speeches, adopting a single recognizable piece of clothing like Jobs’ trademark black turtleneck, and even occasionally teasing “one more thing” for the surprise at the end of their presentations. In the newsroom, we’d sometimes joke about the Jobs wannabes; many were stiff suits who didn’t have the credibility to pull it off.
I thought Huang might be a Jobs wannabe, too, the first time I saw that he’d adopted a black jacket as his uniform. (It was not always a
leather
jacket; an
earlier
version
was a Nvidia-branded softshell.) Huang later insisted on wearing a jacket even when the temperature was hot — more than once, I saw him sweat profusely rather than take it off. Unlike Jobs, he also held quite a few keynotes when he didn’t have much news to share; he liked to repeat the company’s previous accomplishments as if they were brand-new.
But even if Huang didn’t have the same gravitas as Jobs, he did have exciting tech up his sleeves and loved to demo it onstage. He knew how to get people excited about the future of visual computing with eye-opening gaming graphics, physics and lighting demos, and eventually image recognition, AI weather simulations, digital copies of real-world factories, and the robots that can virtually train in them.
His Nvidia tried to educate people about the how and why of GPUs, too; I still remember in 2008 when Nvidia invited the Mythbusters to demo the difference between serial processing and parallel processing
by firing a 1,100-nozzle paintball gun
to “paint” the
Mona Lisa
in one shot.
What I didn’t know back then: Huang
was
a visionary founder. He took Nvidia to fame and fortune through a series of tremendous bets.
In 1996, three years after he cofounded the company at a Denny’s diner, Nvidia nearly went out of business while working on a failed graphics chip for the Sega Dreamcast game console. But even though he didn’t deliver that chip, Huang personally convinced Sega to invest $5 million afterward,
The Wall Street Journal
reported
in 2024.
He then turned around and bet the company again on the Riva 128 PC graphics accelerator, an effort so ambitious he had to lay off over half of Nvidia’s roughly 100 staffers, skip the prototyping stage, and rush it straight to production, and he still only had one month of payroll left by the time it shipped,
The New Yorker
wrote
in 2023. Thankfully, it was a success, selling
a million units in just four months
and paving the way for both the GeForce GPU and
a long-term relationship
with chip fabricator TSMC.
Roughly eight years later, Huang decided it wasn’t enough to be the leader in PC gaming graphics alone.
He bet the company’s entire gross profit
, he told podcaster Lex Fridman, on shipping a new feature inside those graphics cards that no one had asked for: CUDA. It was the ability to use a GPU for
other
kinds of computing tasks beyond graphics, and Huang said it increased the cost of every GeForce graphics card by 50 percent.
“Originally there was no market or market demand for it. It was almost as if they built it because they could,” says Peddie. “Jensen had the vision for what it could be and the courage to pursue it in spite of the opinions of others.”
“NVIDIA was effectively investing in a computing platform that extended far beyond graphics, with no guarantee of a near-term return,” says HotTech analyst Dave Altavilla.
“Huang saw that a GPU was really a parallel computer that happened to render graphics. CUDA turned that insight into a platform, and it’s why NVIDIA was ready when AI arrived,” Mainelli tells me.
It was a bad time for graphics cards to suddenly cost more. When
the Great Recession
hit in 2007–2009, and Nvidia laptop graphics chips also started
failing due to design defects
, the company lost 80 percent of its market value.
But Huang believed in CUDA enough to invest even more. “He literally handed out high-end NVIDIA GPUs to researchers at industry conferences, while the company seeded universities like Stanford with hardware to encourage development on its platform,” says Altavilla. And by 2012, Nvidia’s potential for AI had started to emerge.
That’s when University of Toronto researchers used Nvidia GPUs to train a
prize-winning image-recognition neural network called AlexNet
, which is widely credited for sparking the AI revolution.
Not all of Huang’s visions panned out the way he publicly expected. That AlexNet demo
directly led to Huang’s bets on chips for self-driving cars
, he said, but he didn’t exactly predict AI — CUDA was instead thought of as better and more affordable supercomputing for researchers and scientists. In 2013,
I also wrote about how his grand plan for the future of the company
relied heavily on putting Nvidia chips in your phone, which didn’t pan out.
But that bet on ARM-based phone chips
did
put Nvidia inside every Nintendo Switch and may have helped make future “AI superchips” possible — the latest Nvidia AI server chips have ARM CPU cores. And in 2022, the leaders of the AI revolution launched the most groundbreaking AI tech yet on Nvidia hardware: ChatGPT. Six years earlier, Huang hand-delivered Nvidia’s first purpose-built AI workstation to OpenAI, and by 2022
Microsoft had strung together tens of thousands of Nvidia A100 GPUs
to handle the load.
“Our strategy, ultimately, is to light every single pixel,” Huang said at the March 2013 event where I took this photo.
Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge
Huang projected that Nvidia would power 500 million phones, 200 million tablets, and 50 million cars in the 2017 timeframe.
Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge
“Every time competitors got close, he moved the fight up a level: the chip, then the server, then networking with the $6.9 billion Mellanox deal, then the full rack, all tied together by CUDA,” says Moorhead. “The speed came from how he ran the company,” he adds. “Decisions that took other companies four weeks took Nvidia four days.”
“Decisions that took other companies four weeks took Nvidia four days.”
As Nvidia’s fortunes and profit ballooned — thousands of dollars in pure profit
every single second!
— and as it became clearer that AI would reshape the world in one way or another, something strange happened. Huang became a celebrity. In summer 2024,
The Wall Street Journal
and social media chronicled that he received a hero’s welcome in his birthplace of Taiwan. He stopped over and over to sign autographs, including
one on a woman’s chest
.
In person, at presentations, and in the company’s investor Q&As, I saw the tone shift. People began treating the leather-jacketed man like an actual rockstar instead of a wannabe rockstar, asking for photos and autographs and complimenting him rather than asking tough questions.
It felt like he’d attained Steve Jobs’ infamous
“reality distortion field”
at last — until he popped that bubble himself with his infidelity.
But one fewer reality distortion field in the world isn’t necessarily a bad thing, and as Apple has shown, a company doesn’t go bust just because its charismatic founder is gone.
Tim Cook made Apple the most profitable company in the world
. The question now is: who for Nvidia?
“He was the king,” says Peddie. “Make no mistake – it was the Jensen Huang company. He called all the shots, took all the glory, and shouldered all the
blame.”
Does Nvidia work without Huang?
Even without a named successor, analysts don’t think Nvidia is in big trouble yet.
“This is a stock shock, not a business shock, for the next year. The roadmap and manufacturing are locked in through 2027,” says
Pat Moorhead, Moor Insights & Strategy
. “The question is whether Nvidia keeps inventing at Jensen’s pace once those plans run out. The bigger risk than any rival chip is customers hedging during a vacuum. That is why the next CEO needs technical credibility, an operating model that doesn’t depend on one person, and a plan to protect CUDA.”
“Founder visionary, culture setter, leader, AI industry spokesperson etc., is the real loss. We don’t think anything changes strategically,” says
Creative Strategies analyst Ben Bajarin
.” The product roadmap is set and remains strong, and the next several generations are already in design, in tape-out or on order. NVIDIA is still the company best placed to ship its roadmap at scale, because it has spent years locking up the supply chain behind it, from leading-edge wafers and CoWoS-class packaging to HBM and the rack-level partners. That supply position does not walk out the door with one person.”
“He was the consummate showman, salesman, and visionary for NVIDIA, so he will be hard to replace,” says
IDC analyst Tom Mainelli
. “But the company’s technology road map is sound, and the team behind him is still there. Choosing the right person to replace him

**Google's Gemini 4 Carbon has become the first non-OpenAI model in a while to top the MathArena math benchmark.** It knocked GPT-6.1 Sol from the top spot, while Claude Fable 5.2 came in second, making it potentially one of the most capable publicly available models for math tasks. OpenAI's models, which recently [allegedly solved demanding equations like the Navier-Stokes equations](https://the-decoder.com/openai-reportedly-closes-in-on-solving-the-hodge-conjecture-its-second-millennium-prize-problem/), aren't publicly available yet.

The model also almost never gives up on a task, a trait that can be read as either positive [or negative](https://the-decoder.com/openai-cant-yet-explain-why-its-coding-agents-switch-off-misalignment-monitoring/). In one case, it launched a script that ran for more than eleven hours without checking on its progress. That extra performance comes at a price, though. With the reasoning settings used in testing, Carbon and Fable 5.2 cost roughly 15 and 40 times as much as GPT-6.1 Sol, respectively.

Title: Anthropic says outdated prompting habits are slowing down Claude Opus 5.5

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-says-outdated-prompting-habits-are-slowing-down-claude-opus-5-5/

Published Time: 2026-11-14T16:42:56+00:00

Markdown Content:
**Anyone using Claude Opus 5.5 should first drop several prompting habits carried over from older model generations, according to Anthropic.**

Anthropic says the model, now the default on Pro, Max, Ultra, and Team plans, works differently from its predecessors and that many users hold it back with outdated instructions.

Topping [the list](https://claude.com/resources/articles/using-claude-opus-5-5-as-your-daily-driver-for-knowledge-work) is Anthropic's advice to cut phrases like "think hard" or "think carefully" from prompts. According to the company, the model always reasons on its own and scales its reasoning depth to the task and the selected effort level. In Anthropic's tests, responses without these phrases started faster with no measurable drop in quality.

These phrases date back to the early days of reasoning models, before today's standard adaptive reasoning existed. "Back then," [meaning about a year and a half ago](https://the-decoder.com/openais-o3-model-outperforms-the-newer-gpt-5-model-on-complex-multi-app-office-tasks/), users could sometimes coax more performance out of a model or steer the router this way.

Anthropic also recommends starting at the "Medium" effort level, the default for Opus 5.5. In internal tests, Opus 5.5 on Medium matched the performance of its predecessor Opus 5 on "High," the company says. Higher settings cost more and don't always produce better results. Anthropic advises switching to "High" only when Medium isn't enough, and users can change the setting in the model menu next to the send button.

Anthropic's prompting tips for Opus 5.5 include connecting files and systems, describing the desired end result, dropping "think hard," starting at Medium effort, sharing diagrams directly, naming unwanted design patterns, and sharing your own house style. | Image: Anthropic

Teams that previously used the cheaper Sonnet and reserved Opus for complex projects should rethink that approach, according to Anthropic. The company argues that a more capable model can finish a task in fewer steps, which can partly [offset](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/optimizing-for-cost-and-intelligence) its higher per-token price. Anyone who regularly cranks Sonnet up to "Extra High" or "Max" effort ends up paying about as much as with Opus 5.5, Anthropic says.

## From chatting to setting goals

Anthropic advises describing the desired result in a single message rather than giving instructions one at a time, covering the goal, the output format, and when the model should check back with questions. Opus 5.5 is better than its predecessor at seeing multi-part tasks through, according to the company. The model can increasingly take over the back-and-forth users used to handle in the chat, sometimes doing it better, and effectively prompt itself from a single initial input.

Anthropic recommends attaching diagrams and tables as images or files instead of typing them out. Workarounds that older models required, such as manually transcribing chart values, are no longer needed, the company says.

Users who need a finished document or spreadsheet should ask for it directly instead of requesting a draft first. Opus 5.5 often goes from request to finished product in a single pass, the company says. Image reading also improved significantly in Opus 5.5. Even at the lowest effort level, it read values from dense charts more accurately than Opus 5 at the highest, the firm says.

## Naming specific styles works better than banning generic design

For design tasks, Anthropic recommends naming unwanted styles specifically, such as a cream-colored background or pill-shaped buttons, rather than vaguely banning "generic design." According to the company, general instructions only swap one default style for another.

Users who connect Claude to their own files and systems through connectors get significantly more tailored results, Anthropic says, because the model can pull in the information it needs on its own.

Title: OpenAI reassigns robotics researchers to other teams as general-purpose models might make specialized robotics AI unnecessary

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/openai-reassigns-robotics-researchers-to-other-teams-as-general-purpose-models-might-make-specialized-robotics-ai-unnecessary/

Published Time: 2026-11-14T11:40:51+00:00

Markdown Content:
**OpenAI has reorganized its robotics team, though for different reasons than when it first disbanded the unit in 2020.**

Rather than abandoning robotics, the company wants to accelerate it by folding researchers into other teams. Robotics researchers are moving to the main research team under Chief Research Officer Mark Chen, while the applied robotics and hardware teams join Greg Brockman's Applied organization.

OpenAI made the decision on such short notice that it had already booked a booth at the [Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL)](https://www.corl.org/) in Austin, which then sat empty, [Fortune reports](https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/openai-disbands-robotics-team-as-its-general-models-start-running-robots/). OpenAI apparently believes that general-purpose models like [GPT-6 Astra can control robots directly](https://the-decoder.com/gpt-6-astra-appears-to-show-a-step-change-in-spatial-reasoning-based-on-early-benchmarks/), reducing the need for specialized robotics models.

In [an Nvidia study](https://research.nvidia.com/labs/srl/projects/astranomy/), an Astra-powered agent achieved a 74.8 percent success rate on simulated robotics tasks, compared to 51 percent for the best specialized models. The tests used a simulated DROID robot, not a physical one.

A new [robotics benchmark called StationeryBench](https://github.com/robocurve/stationerybench) compared GPT-6 Astra with Ai2's MolmoAct2 on five tasks involving desk objects on dual-arm YAM robotic arms. Across 200 trials, Astra fully completed 7 out of 100 tasks, while MolmoAct2 didn't complete a single one. Astra's average progress score was 46, compared to 12 for MolmoAct2. In another test, [Astra running on a humanoid robot](https://the-decoder.com/researchers-plug-gpt-6-astra-directly-into-a-robot-and-let-it-clean-up-an-unfamiliar-kitchen/) navigated and cleaned up a kitchen.

It remains unclear how much robotics data OpenAI and others incorporated during training. Other large general-purpose models from [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/research/claude-plays-robotics) and [Google](https://the-decoder.com/google-wants-gemini-4-argon-to-be-the-only-ai-model-robots-need/) have also made recent progress on robotics tasks. Specialized robotics models may still have advantages in [cost and reliability](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22839395) as well as [speed and energy consumption](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18374), even if they don't generalize as well.

[Yoav Artzi](https://x.com/yoavartzi), an AI researcher at Cornell University and Google DeepMind, also [sees Astra as a major leap in spatial understanding](https://x.com/yoavartzi/status/2098496429752713618). On the still-unpublished REMAP benchmark, GPT-6 Astra reaches near-human accuracy, according to Artzi. He [suspects](https://x.com/yoavartzi/status/2098511167090000086) that OpenAI may have trained the model on large amounts of 3D training data such as Blender scenes.

## OpenAI and robots, it's complicated

OpenAI shut down its robotics division in 2020 because, according to co-founder Wojciech Zaremba, the company lacked the training data it needed and large language models were a faster path to AGI. The company rebuilt the team in 2024. [CEO Sam Altman is reportedly targeting a first public robot demo for 2027](https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/openai-disbands-robotics-team-as-its-general-models-start-running-robots/), and OpenAI wants to [build its own everyday robots](https://the-decoder.com/openai-starts-with-infrastructure-robots-but-aims-for-everyone-having-a-personal-robot-doing-anything-they-need/) in the long term. But the company also faces heavy financial pressure to [focus on its core AI business](https://the-decoder.com/openais-sora-burned-a-million-dollars-a-day-while-losing-half-its-users-in-record-time/), where it has [lost significant ground to Anthropic](https://the-decoder.com/anthropics-ipo-is-six-times-oversubscribed-and-on-track-to-become-the-largest-public-offering-in-history/).

Title: Anthropic can already retrain Mythos with "a fraction of the compute originally needed," says former researcher Coxon

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-can-already-retrain-mythos-with-a-fraction-of-the-compute-originally-needed-says-former-researcher-coxon/

Published Time: 2026-11-14T11:21:41+00:00

Markdown Content:
**Jacob Coxon, former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher who brought AI fears into the mainstream, says a slide from Anthropic's IPO roadshow was a major reason he quit.**

Coxon says a slide [Anthropic released for its IPO roadshow](https://the-decoder.com/anthropics-ipo-filing-shows-soaring-revenue-mounting-costs-and-existential-risks/) was a key reason he left the company after only about four months. The chart shows how much compute Anthropic needs over time to train its models, and the axis is compressed so that a 10x and a 100x increase barely look different.

Yet the curve still climbs steeply, which [Coxon says](https://x.com/hilbertspaess/status/2121425977876341092) shows that algorithmic efficiency is improving not just quickly but at an accelerating rate. "It's an insane plot and I'm surprised they made it public," he writes.

Coxon argues that Anthropic's [Mythos](https://the-decoder.com/from-gpt-2-to-claude-mythos-the-return-of-ai-models-deemed-too-dangerous-to-release/) model, a major capability jump in the spring, was part of this accelerating trend. "Mythos was not a one-time deviation, but a point on a superexponential. They could already retrain Mythos with a fraction of the compute originally needed," he writes.

This slide from Anthropic's IPO roadshow shows the "Pre-training compute multiplier" for code over time. The y-axis is logarithmic. Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon says the steep climb from July 2024 to October 2026 points to superexponential algorithmic progress. Anthropic notes that the data points are based on internal estimates and are for illustration only. | Image: Anthropic

He says algorithmic improvements are "on the verge of being automated," which is why he wants frontier model development paused next year so competitors can catch up. A pause, he writes, would "commoditize human-level intelligence. It would only harm OpenAI and Anthropic."

Coxon previously trained AI models at OpenAI and, most recently, Anthropic. He drew wide attention in September with [public warnings about the risks of advanced AI systems](https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-scientist-puts-the-odds-of-ai-destroying-humanity-above-ten-percent-this-decade/), echoed by other protagonists in the industry. One of their fears is that advanced, self-improving AI could get out of control.

Runway's open-source Praxis-1 turns video AI into a robot controller
Tomislav Bezmalinović
Nov 14, 2026
Runway
Key Points
Runway has released its robot model Praxis-1 with open weights and source code under the Apache 2.0 license.
Trained on videos and robot data, the model processes camera images, text instructions, and position data to calculate matching robot movements.
Praxis-1 can be adapted to new robot systems through additional training, according to Runway. The model does occasionally confuse similar-looking objects, though, and it can't yet reliably plan complex action sequences on its own.
Ask about this article…
Search
AI company Runway has released its robot model Praxis-1 with open weights and source code. The model uses what it learned from video to control robots and shows promising results in the company's own tests.
Runway has released Praxis-1, its AI model for controlling robots. The company first introduced Praxis-1 in late September but initially gave access only to select partners. Alongside the release, Runway published a detailed research report with new performance tests.
Runway's model weights and source code are available under the Apache 2.0 license, which allows commercial use.
Ad
Praxis-1 takes in camera images, text instructions, and information about a robot's position. From those inputs, it predicts how the environment will change and calculates the right robot movements. As new camera frames come in, the model continuously adjusts its control.
Ad
Praxis-1 builds on video training to control robots
Praxis-1 builds on a video model that learned how objects move and interact from ordinary footage. Runway then fine-tuned it with videos of human actions and robot data. This approach could reduce the need for expensive robot-specific datasets, which have traditionally been collected just to train these kinds of systems.
Runway is best known for generative video models like
Gen-4.5
. With Praxis-1, the company is bringing its video research into robotics. Runway calls Praxis-1 a
World Action Model
that predicts how a scene will change and derives matching robot movements from those predictions. Since September, robotics companies Standard Bots, Noble Machines, and Ultra have been testing Praxis-1 on different systems, including a humanoid robot, an industrial robot arm, and a dual-arm warehouse robot.
Ad
Praxis-1 leads among World Action Models
Praxis-1 still needs some specialized robot data. To adapt it to a Franka robot arm, Runway used about 277 hours of recordings from the public DROID research dataset, according to its
research report
. Those recordings show robots grasping and moving objects, for example. For a dual-arm robot, the company used between 1,400 and 2,600 hours of training material. Runway had already used DROID data and data from other robot systems during earlier training stages. Whether the approach actually needs less robot data overall than comparable models without general video pretraining is still an open question.
On
Nvidia's RoboLab-120 leaderboard
, Praxis-1 scores a 46.2 percent success rate. The benchmark tests how reliably robot models can sort, grasp, or stack objects across 120 tasks in simulation.
FLUX 3 Action
, also built as a World Action Model, scores 42.9 percent under the same test conditions. That puts Praxis-1 at the top of the World Action Model category. In the overall leaderboard, it ranks fifth behind two AI agents and two robot models with different architectures. Runway ran all the tests itself, and the results haven't been independently verified yet.
Ad
After fine-tuning on DROID data, Runway tested the model on a real Franka robot arm. Both models had to complete the same ten tasks, like placing a banana on a plate or closing a drawer. With ten attempts per task, Praxis-1 succeeded 88 times, while FLUX 3 Action managed 80.
Ad
Runway also tested how well Praxis-1 transfers to a robot type it had never seen before, using data from a mobile robot platform with a gripper arm that Google had previously used to develop
RT-1
. Recordings from this robot weren't part of Praxis-1's earlier training. After fine-tuning on about 95 hours of robot data, the model hit an average success rate of 80 percent in simulated tests, according to Runway. The tests covered four types of tasks, including grabbing soda cans, opening and closing drawers, and placing an apple in a drawer. Google's original RT-1 model scored 52.4 percent on the same benchmark.
Praxis-1 still has clear limits
Developers can download Praxis-1 from
Hugging Face
after signing up and agreeing to the access terms. The
code is on GitHub
. According to
Runway's announcement
, pre-adapted versions for different robots are already available alongside the base model. The base model needs additional training before it can work with new robot systems.
The standard model version needs a GPU with 80 GB of memory. A compressed version should fit on an RTX 5090 with 32 GB of VRAM based on Runway's memory estimates, though the actual peak memory usage hasn't been measured yet according to the GitHub docs.
The model sometimes confuses similar-looking objects and struggles with vague instructions, according to Runway's research report. For longer tasks, individual steps need to be spelled out because Praxis-1 can't reliably plan complex action sequences on its own yet.
Runway sees Praxis-1 primarily as a system for fast execution of robot movements. In the future, it could work alongside general-purpose AI models that break complex tasks down into individual steps.

WeightSpace
, an optimizer that plugs into any DSPy program and metric. In Cmpnd’s tests, about $5 to $10 of GPT-6-Astra calls improved every decision model they tried. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our

TL;DR
What it is:
A DSPy optimizer (
WeightSpace
) where a writer LLM edits a student model’s weights. MIT license,
pip install dspy-wsp
, needs DSPy 3.5.
Size:
Tested on open decision models from 0.6B to 9B parameters. One 25-pass run edited a single layer or head.
Runs on:
One Mac for all experiments. 2B models used about 6 GB of memory. d1-omni-600M needs 4 GB or more (Mac or GPU).
Performance:
WeightSpace alone added 1.9 to 16.1 points on Typed Decisions. With ReAnchor, gains were 6.5 to 20.0 points.
Best:
d1-omni-600M rose from 50.9% to 69.1% (+18.3) with WeightSpace + ReAnchor.
Worst:
Clef-Flash (9B) gained only +1.9 from WeightSpace alone. With the original paper’s stricter rule, d1-omni-600M gained just +2.8.
Bottom line:
Best: a cheap, gradient-free edit that ships as a small, verifiable patch. Worst: very experimental, slow (78 to 167 minutes per run) and weakest on larger models.
What is weight-space programming?
Weight-space programming (WSP) treats a neural network’s weights as a program that can be read and rewritten. The idea comes from MIT research:
Sparks of Weight-Space Programming
.
A frontier model (the research team used GPT-6-Astra) looks at weight tensors, reasons about what each part computes, and changes them to match a goal written in plain English. The research team stresses that WSP names an emerging capability, not a fixed method. Gradients were banned in their experiments, but the concept does not rule them out.
How is it different from fine-tuning or prompt optimization?
It helps to compare the 3 levers developers usually pull:
Prompt optimization
(DSPy’s MIPROv2,
GEPA
) edits text: instructions and examples. The model’s weights never change.
Fine-tuning
(DSPy’s BootstrapFinetune, used inside
BetterTogether
) changes weights with gradient descent. It needs training data, a training loop and usually a GPU.
Weight-space programming
changes weights by reasoning. The editor forms a hypothesis (“these neurons over-score option B”), writes code to patch them, and checks the result with a few forward passes.
The
research post
frames WSP as the next step after using LLMs to optimize text artifacts. Earlier work let LLMs hill-climb on prompts, harnesses and training code. Weights were left to Adam or to trained weight-generating networks. WSP argues LLM reasoning can now reach the weights directly.
What did the original research show?
The MIT team ran 9 experiments. Several are striking:
Reading weights:
Astra named the correct game (Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, Freeway) for 4 PPO policy networks from weights alone.
Fixing a broken policy:
A Kinetix car-on-ramp policy failed all 256 episodes. One edit to 3.5% of its weights made it succeed in all 1,024 test episodes.
Writing from zero:
On MinAtar Breakout, a zero-initialized network written in 1 shot scored 517.4. PPO reached 25.3 after 500M steps.
Fixing an LLM:
Qwen3.5-0.8B looped on math problems. Astra traced the issue to MLP layers 15 and 19 and changed 131,072 weights (0.016% of the model). With 50 forward passes, MATH-500 rose from 7.9% to 48.1% and GSM8K from 13.8% to 67.1%.
The research also shows limits. On Gemma 3 270M, edits moved MATH-500 from 6.8% to between 7.0% and 7.7%. The research team did not count that as a real gain. Editing can remove an obstacle, but it could not add a missing ability.
How does dspy-wsp work?
dspy-wsp turns that research loop into a standard DSPy optimizer.
The
GitHub Repo
describes 3 actors:
The student:
the small model your DSPy program runs on. Its weights load into a local Python process.
The writer:
a frontier LLM, recommended as
gpt-6-astra
at maximum reasoning effort.
The sandbox:
a kernel where the writer runs code. macOS uses built-in
sandbox-exec
; Linux uses bubblewrap.
The writer works in turns. Each turn has a short explanation, then 1 code block.
That block is either:
a
Python block
that reads or edits weights inside the sandbox, or
a
forward block
that runs your DSPy program on practice examples.
Forward passes come from a fixed budget (
max_passes=25
in the tests). When the budget runs out, the writer’s best edit becomes the patch. A hidden validation set then compares original and edited weights on the same examples and seeds.
What data does the writer see?
The repo is explicit about data separation:
trainset
is the writer’s practice set.
holdout
moves a fraction (0.25 in the example) of training data into a check set. The writer can score edits on it but never sees the examples.
valset
stays hidden and runs once at the end.
Metrics can return
dspy.Prediction(score=..., feedback=...)
. The feedback text is visible to the writer.
What did the writer actually change?
The
results write-up
lists every edit. The edits are small and targeted:

What does the code look like?
The
Repo example
triages support tickets. The signature uses only decision-type outputs:
Copy Code
Copied

import dspy
from typing import Literal
from dspy_wsp import WeightSpace, load_decision_backend

class Triage(dspy.Signature):
    """Triage a support ticket."""
    ticket: str = dspy.InputField()
    urgent: bool = dspy.OutputField(desc="Does this ticket need a reply today?")
    team: Literal["billing", "technical", "account"] = dspy.OutputField(desc="Which team should handle it?")

backend = load_decision_backend("d1")   # d1-omni-600M
optimizer = WeightSpace(
    metric=metric,
    writer_lm=dspy.LM("openai/gpt-6-astra", model_type="responses", reasoning_effort="max"),
    backend=backend,
    max_passes=25,
    holdout=0.25,
    run_dir="runs/triage",
)
compiled = optimizer.compile(dspy.Predict(Triage), trainset=train, valset=test)
compiled(ticket="I was charged twice this month.")   # runs on the edited weights
After
compile
, the program calls the edited local model instead of a hosted API.
compiled.wsp_patch.summary()
shows what changed.
How well does it work? Typed Decisions benchmark results
Cmpnd tested on
Typed Decisions
, a benchmark for typed probabilistic decisions. A model reads 1 piece of unstructured state and answers 5 typed questions at once. Each answer is a probability distribution. The test split has 400 cases and 2,000 decisions.
Each model got 25 forward passes from GPT-6-Astra. Gains are paired, with a standard error of ±0.7 to 1.4 points.

for d1-omni-600M, d1-2B and Clef-Flash;
results README
for NanoJev.
ReAnchor
is an earlier Cmpnd optimizer. Decision models output probabilities, and thresholds turn those into answers. ReAnchor refits each question’s thresholds with no LLM calls. WeightSpace changes the model; ReAnchor recalibrates its output. The 2 stack well.
Three patterns stand out:
WeightSpace beat ReAnchor alone on every model shown.
On d1-omni-600M, it added +16.1 versus +9.3.
The largest model gained least.
The 9B Clef-Flash gained only +1.9 from WeightSpace alone.
The combination matters most at 9B.
Clef-Flash jumped to +6.5 when both optimizers ran.
Does the writer model matter?
The answer is yes. With
gpt-6.1-sol
as the writer, WeightSpace alone gave +5.8 on d1-omni-600M, +12.1 on NanoJev and −0.6 on d1-2B. Astra produced +16.1, +13.3 and +13.4 on the same models.
Did dspy-wsp bend the original paper’s rules?
Slightly, and Cmpnd says so. By default, the writer can recompute the decision head inside its kernel. Setting
simulate_head=False
enforces the paper’s stricter rule. Under that rule, d1-omni-600M gained only +2.8 ± 0.7 points. Adding ReAnchor brought it to +9.3, no better than ReAnchor alone.
How do you deploy an edited model?
Each run writes a patch to

. The patch holds

and

Programs:
compiled.save("program.json")
and reload with

.
The edited model runs locally. On Apple silicon it uses MLX. On Linux it uses PyTorch, on an NVIDIA GPU if present.

articles.summary_ko: , an open-source memory system for LLMs. The Memorilla memory system reads a whole document collection and hands a frozen LLM just 16 memory tokens. Stanford researchers have released
Memorilla
, an open-source memory system for LLMs. The Memorilla memory system reads a whole document collection and hands a frozen LLM just 16 memory tokens. On FactKG, a frozen Qwen3-8B scored 84.33% with Memorilla, against 80.43% with every
document in context
. It did that with 108x fewer document tokens. Code, training recipes and checkpoints are public under
Apache 2.0
. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our
GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension
.
TL;DR
Size:
194M-parameter trainable memory module. It always outputs 16 memory tokens, whatever the collection size. The encoder (
Qwen3-Embedding-4B
) and decoder (
Qwen3-8B
) stay frozen.
Runs on:
Linux with CUDA GPUs and Python 3.11. The quickstart needs 1 GPU with 80 GB (recipes ran on H100 80GB). No quantized variants disclosed.
Performance:
Highest reported average across 8 benchmarks (49.68), top score on 5 of 8.
Best:
PersonaMem-v2 accuracy of 44.60%, versus 27.92% for full context.
Worst:
PubMedQA accuracy of 59.00%, versus 69.00% for LLMLingua-2.
What is Memorilla?
Memorilla is a memory module that turns a document collection into 16 vectors for a frozen LLM. The work comes from Jure Leskovec’s SNAP group, with co-authors from Toronto, Penn and MIT.
A frozen LLM can only use what sits in its context window. Full-context prompting grows slower as history grows. Retrieval pastes the chunks most similar to the question, and can miss weaker clues. Memorilla takes a third route: it learns what each question needs from the whole store.
How does Memorilla work?
The pipeline has 3 steps:
Encode once.
A frozen Qwen3-Embedding-4B embeds each document a single time. New documents never force re-encoding of old ones.
Read per question.
16 learned slots attend to the question and the full store. The module uses 2 cross-attention layers with 8 heads.
Inject.
The slots are projected into Qwen3-8B’s input embedding space and prepended to the question.
Only the memory module trains: 194,123,776 parameters for the 8B decoder. Training runs in 3 stages. Stage 1 uses about 1.98M Wikipedia paraphrase-reconstruction examples. Stage 2 adds about 1.34M examples from 10 QA and summarization datasets. Stage 3 fine-tunes on all 8 benchmarks. The full recipe takes about 19 hours on 4 H100 GPUs.
How does Memorilla perform on benchmarks?
All baselines use the same frozen Qwen3-8B, per the paper’s main table. Scores are self-reported by the research team.
FactKG:
84.33% accuracy, versus 80.43% full context and 80.38% MemoRAG.
PersonaMem-v2:
44.60%, versus 30.90% for xRAG, the next best method.
TriviaQA:
57.00 exact match, just ahead of MemoRAG at 56.60.
LaMP-4 / LaMP-7:
18.15 and 48.37 ROUGE-L, both the best scores.
Average:
49.68, versus 41.92 for xRAG, 40.75 for LLMLingua-2 and 38.02 for Mem0.

What is Vercel UI SDK?
UI SDK is a library of UI behaviors from Vercel Labs that agents assemble into components. The
README
lists keyboard navigation, focus, selection, dismissal, popups, drag and drop, and the ARIA they need. All of it lives in
@ui-sdk/core

The
project site

How does UI SDK work?
Components start as primitives defined with
definePrimitive
. A primitive declares state, an API and slots. Slots attach attributes, events and behaviors to DOM parts. The README example builds a search field with
createFocusRecovery
. Its Clear button appears only when there is text.
Each framework then renders the primitive with

. The README says the parts are the same in all 5 adapters. So 1 behavior definition can serve a React app and a Svelte app.

: type a few letters to jump to an item

,

createViewport

Title: Lovable: Many Apps Expose Sensitive Data

URL Source: https://www.crissyfield.de/research/lovable-en/

Markdown Content:
## Lovable: Many Apps Built on the Platform Expose Sensitive Data

**AI makes it easier to build your own web applications, but handling sensitive data still requires special care. We examined 159,041 Lovable projects and found many cases where personal and confidential information was accessible without logging in.**

## About Lovable

Lovable is a Swedish AI startup founded in Stockholm in 2023 by Anton Osika and Fabian Hedin. The platform turns plain-language descriptions into web applications and is designed to be accessible even to _people with little or no programming experience_.

Lovable grew out of Osika’s open-source project “GPT Engineer”, released in 2023. The project evolved into the GPT Engineer App before being renamed Lovable in late 2024 and launching publicly that November.

## The Promise

Lovable can build impressively sophisticated web projects with AI, from static websites to full applications with user management and database connections. But as soon as an application handles confidential information, one question becomes crucial: **Is that data protected against unauthorized access?**

[In its marketing](https://lovable.dev/blog/what-is-vibe-coding), [Lovable repeatedly](https://lovable.dev/blog/2025-01-30-why-non-tech-founders-no-longer-need-a-developer-to-launch-software)[emphasizes](https://lovable.dev/en/founders)[that no technical knowledge is needed to build projects](https://lovable.dev/vibecoding). This can give the impression that the platform takes care of security too. Yet Lovable’s Terms & Conditions place responsibility for applications and data handling on the customers themselves.

That leaves a troubling gap between the promise of an easy-to-use, all-in-one service and the responsibilities customers are expected to take on.

Against this backdrop, we investigated how well sensitive data in Lovable applications is protected, in collaboration with [Handelsblatt](https://www.handelsblatt.com/). [Lina Knees reported on the findings on November 2, 2026 (in German)](https://www.handelsblatt.com/technik/ki/lovable-experten-finden-datenluecke-bei-beliebter-ki-coding-plattform/100264923.html).

## Research Question

We wanted to find out whether sensitive data in Lovable applications was accessible without logging in. We looked separately at data sent when a website first loaded and additional content we checked by making further read-only requests with the same API key.

The result: **We found many clear examples of sensitive data left unprotected.**

## Methodology

We focused on the database service [Supabase](https://supabase.com/). Its integration is relatively easy to analyze, and we believe it is the most widely used database service among Lovable projects. Lovable’s own database features, introduced in late 2025, are still less widely used. Similar misconfigurations may occur there too, but we did not examine them in this analysis.

Using datasets from the open web archive [Common Crawl](https://commoncrawl.org/), we identified and analyzed **159,041 Lovable projects** from _December 2025 to September 2026_. Of these, 34,545 used Supabase.

**24,664 websites** sent database records from Supabase as soon as they loaded, without requiring a login or any other interaction. That alone is not a security issue: the data may be intended for public display. But by making additional read-only requests, we were able to retrieve more database content. We found records containing email addresses in **10,560 tables** across **7,403** of the 24,664 websites (30%).

## Limitations

Email addresses can help identify records containing personal data, but they may also be public contact addresses or test data. At the same time, this approach misses personal records that contain no email address. These effects partly offset one another, though we could not establish to what extent. The 30% figure should therefore not be read as a confirmed data leak rate. It applies only to the 24,664 websites we examined more closely. Our sample, drawn from Common Crawl, is also not representative of all Lovable applications.

We retrieved only parts of the datasets rather than downloading them in full. The figures below reflect the records we actually downloaded; the affected datasets may contain more. We are not publishing details of how to access them, as doing so could make further access easier.

## Data Leaks

We found many serious cases of exposed data, including:

*   A German lifestyle forum exposed **more than 80,000 profiles** containing full names, email addresses, dates of birth, and gender information. **More than 200,000 chat messages** were also accessible.

*   Several event organizers and restaurants exposed **tens of thousands of records relating to ticket and food sales**, with no login required. The records we inspected included email addresses, phone numbers, postal addresses, payment information, and ticket codes.

*   A property management company exposed AI-generated summaries of internal emails containing sensitive information about tenants, property owners, and business partners.

*   In a particularly serious case, a service provider exposed **more than 1,000 records containing identity document details**, including **passport numbers**, **expiration dates**, and **nationalities**. These highly sensitive identity details could be used for identity theft.

*   Other accessible content included tens of thousands of **contracts**, **invoices**, **personal photo albums**, and **internal WhatsApp communications**.

*   We also found numerous newsletter subscriptions, waiting lists, and contact and support inquiries. In one case, **280,000 emails sent** to a provider’s customers were accessible.

Depending on what it contains, exposed data like this could be used for phishing, ticket fraud, or identity theft. We could not establish whether any of it had been misused.

Handelsblatt contacted Lovable with the findings of our investigation.

## Implications

Our analysis shows that many Lovable applications leave even highly sensitive data unprotected, with potentially serious consequences for the people affected.

Access control mistakes can happen in any application, whether written by people or built with AI. With Lovable, database integrations follow recurring patterns, making it easier for attackers to look for similar misconfigurations across many applications. An approach that works against one app may then work against others with little extra effort. Users without a technical background also face a harder task spotting and preventing these flaws.

An easy-to-use development platform does not remove the need for an expert review of access permissions before an application handles confidential data.

Automated checks **are no substitute for a professional security assessment**.

Before an application handles real customer or business data, its access permissions, interfaces, and separation between user accounts should be reviewed. These checks should be repeated after significant changes. If the necessary expertise is not available in-house, bring in qualified support.

If you would like help securing your application, please get in touch.

_Note: This research report presents a more recent analysis and updated figures compared with the Handelsblatt article published on November 2, 2026._
