Title: Tech Companies Are Trying to Shift the Entire Concept of Privacy (Again)

URL Source: https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/11/tech-companies-are-trying-shift-entire-concept-privacy-again

Published Time: 2026-11-13T13:29:31-08:00

Markdown Content:
Privacy, which companies were once happy to claim was all about personal choice, is now primed to affect everyone around you even more than it already did.

[Meta](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/03/think-twice-buying-or-using-metas-ray-bans) and [Google’s](https://9to5google.com/2026/11/12/google-intelligent-eyewear-glasses/) smart glasses can record anything the owner is looking at or use artificial intelligence to describe it. Apple’s* [Audio Intelligence feature](https://support.apple.com/en-us/148354) turns every Apple Watch into a transcription machine that records or summarizes your day. [Amazon’s Bee devices](https://bee.computer/products/frontier) take that a step further and can record and transcribe everything. Dozens of other companies are introducing [pendants](https://www.forbes.com/sites/forbes-personal-shopper/article/best-ai-wearables/), [rings](https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/20/voccis-ring-adds-a-new-form-factor-to-meeting-note-taking/), and [other products](https://www.amazon.com/b?ie=UTF8&node=223193081011) designed to record, transcribe, or summarize everything we say and do all day long.

Privacy has always been a team sport. The actions you take with [communication apps](https://ssd.eff.org/module/communicating-others), [collaborative software](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2018/10/privacy-badger-now-fights-more-sneaky-google-tracking), or [your cloud backup solutions](https://fixitalready.eff.org/apple/#/), have long impacted everyone else you’re interacting with. But moving those choices deeper into the physical world where strangers, colleagues, family, and friends are _all_ now a part of your privacy choices is drastically changing the game.

Tech companies want us to accept a reality where one person’s privacy choices (or lack thereof) means you suddenly need to be an expert in consumer tech who understands the capabilities of many devices on the market, how they work, how and if they signal when they’re recording, and what platforms they do or do not connect to. They believe these ambient surveillance devices that work in the background and are designed to look as normal as possible are the future, while they also expect the owners of these devices to use them responsibly and to notify those around them of their capabilities to act within whatever laws their states may have.

This is not reasonable, nor how consent works in any practical sense.

Let’s break this down by looking at some of the biggest players currently in the game: Apple and Amazon, who have two different takes on transcribing audio throughout the day, as well as Meta and Google, who both have slapped AI and cameras onto eyeglasses.

## How to Think About the Technical Promises Companies Make

Ask Apple about privacy concerns and they’ll [point to a white paper](https://www.apple.com/privacy/docs/Audio_Intelligence_Privacy_Overview_Sep_2026.pdf) that explains all the technical barriers between them as a company and the data generated by the watch. Ask Meta and they’ll talk about all the ways you can [customize the privacy controls](https://www.meta.com/ai-glasses/privacy/) or how certain details, like faces, may be blurred out when you interact with Meta AI through the glasses (but not during standard recording). [Google does this too](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/safety-security/intelligent-eyewear-privacy-protections/). Amazon will also talk about how [you’re always in control](https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/devices/amazon-personal-ai-bee-frontier-bee-eclipse), and no audio is stored (though it’ll also let you enable Amazon store integration, so your conversations can directly result in ads for products). And so on across all the companies making these products.

Some of these solutions do a better job than others at cutting out potential law enforcement or company access to this data. There will be a time to dive into these details more deeply, but the technical privacy promises these companies focus on only cover the consumer and user of the device. They ignore every bystander you interact with and their inability to actually opt out. There is no technical protection for you as a non-user of these devices, the person who finds yourself captured by them.

Still, we hope to look deeper into the technical differences between this category of devices soon.

## There Must Be Some Laws to Consider, Right?

With something like Apple’s Audio Intelligence and Amazon’s Bee devices, it may be best to treat them similar to an always-recording microphone, even if companies try to claim there’s “technically” no audio recording. These tools still often use a microphone to capture raw audio from [conversations](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/2510) and convert it into summaries or transcripts before discarding the audio. Google's [blog post notes that it has](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/safety-security/intelligent-eyewear-privacy-protections/)whole responsible use part of their Terms of Service where users have to agree not to record others without permission or in sensitive places.

But it’s not just the question of the legality from the point of view of the user. Law enforcement will eventually try to compel access to the data that these products create (either real-time audio or the summaries and transcripts they create). And while some products, like Apple’s Audio Intelligence, are engineered to make that difficult, not every product will be. We know from history that when data exists, governments will do everything they can to access it. There’s no reason to think something would change today.

## No Tech and Legal Solutions Will Reduce Social Issues

There is a problem humming along in the background that is impossible to address with technical or legal solutions. If secretly documenting conversations becomes the norm, it makes every private conversation less spontaneous and open. It breaks a longstanding social norm that you will not record and document every conversation with friends, family, colleagues, or strangers.

The companies that make these sorts of products like to claim they’re no different from tools we already have. You can easily record everything right now with a phone or a camera. Heck, you can do so with a camcorder or cassette recorder if you want. And you can transcribe conversations with pen and paper, too. But those are actionable steps we take that both require effort from the user, and are clear to others around us. This new wave of passive surveillance tech is designed to encourage continuous monitoring and hide its use.

Even taken at face value, none of these products can understand the complex social context we all navigate every day. We intrinsically know there are different social agreements we all make when we’re standing on a street corner, at a protest, in a bathroom, at a doctor’s office, at the gym, or in a restaurant. Taking notes in a meeting at work is completely normal. Getting a summary of a conversation with your best friend about their divorce is not. Always-on monitoring of our conversations is an unacceptable burden on our conversational privacy.

Google seems to all but admit this problem in a [conversation with CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/12/tech/google-glasses-privacy-concerns) when it described the company’s experiments with a notification system that would alert people’s phones when someone was recording nearby:

> “And just alerting bystanders doesn’t do much to help, [Juston Payne, senior director of product management at Google] said. “It can actually be weirdly disempowering to you in that you’re like, ‘What am I meant to do now?’” he said.”

## What We Can Do About It

It’s easy to buy into the tech company line that these products are inevitable, but we’ve seen so many vaporware products over the years that we should take those claims of success with a grain of salt. We’ve seen entire product categories come and go within just a few years, and if the public doesn’t want this stuff, the tech companies will have to throw in the towel.

Of course, that doesn’t mean we all just have to sit around and hope that’s what happens. For its part, Apple [launched its Audio Intelligence features in beta](https://9to5mac.com/2026/11/03/watchos-27-3-beta-adds-new-siri-recap-and-live-rewind-features-for-apple-watch/) specifically to get feedback, and we think it’s worth taking the time to [fill out their feedback forms](https://www.apple.com/feedback/watch/) (or in the [Feedback Assistant app](https://developer.apple.com/feedback-assistant/#feedback-assistant) if you’re in the beta) and let them know what you think.

Products from the likes of Meta, Google, Amazon, and others might be harder to push back on, [but politely and clearly engaging](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/03/think-twice-buying-or-using-metas-ray-bans) with those who use them in ways that make you uncomfortable is a good place to start. And if you see abusive videos on social networks where these sorts of products are used, report them. If you find these products useful for yourself, make it clear to those around you when you’re using them, and only do so with consent and in social moments where it makes sense to do so.

*Apple is an EFF donor. EFF donors do not influence our agenda or our positions.

articles.content:
Title: When One GPU Isn’t Enough: Serving GLM-5.3 Across Two NVIDIA DGX Stations with vLLM

URL Source: https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/when-one-gpu-isnt-enough-serving-glm-5-3-across-two-nvidia-dgx-stations-with-vllm/

Published Time: 2026-11-13T17:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
Running a frontier-scale model locally means keeping all its weights in GPU memory; the largest models no longer fit on one machine. Two NVIDIA DGX Stations connected over ConnectX-8 RDMA serve one model through a single endpoint, with tensor parallelism splitting the model weights and computation across both GPUs.

The NVIDIA [GLM-5.3 NVFP4](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/GLM-5.3-NVFP4) model, a quantized version of [Z.ai](http://z.ai/)’s mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, has 753 billion parameters, with 40 billion activated per token. Sparse activation reduces computation, but all model weights still need to remain available because each token can be routed to different experts. At about 464 GB, the checkpoint exceeds the 252 GB of HBM3e on a single GB300 GPU. This tutorial uses two DGX Stations to keep the weights in GPU memory, with CPU weight offload disabled.

Before starting, connect the two Stations with the [Connect Two DGX Stations playbook](https://build.nvidia.com/station/connect-two-stations).

This post shows how to serve GLM-5.3 locally across two NVIDIA DGX Stations with vLLM, send a request, and measure behavior under concurrent load. Tensor parallelism (TP=2) splits the model’s tensors across the two GB300 GPUs. Both Stations compute every request, and Station A returns the answer through one OpenAI-compatible API. By the end, you’ll have a working endpoint and a baseline for how it behaves under load.

_Figure 1. Two Stations serve one model: each GPU holds and computes part of the model over the selected RDMA connection. Their memories remain distinct_

## Prerequisites

*   Two GB300 DGX Stations running Linux, connected and validated with the [Connect Two DGX Stations playbook](https://build.nvidia.com/station/connect-two-stations), including its GPU-memory RDMA test on both rails.
*   SSH and sudo access on both Stations with the same Linux username. Docker and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit come preinstalled with the [DGX Station software stack](https://docs.nvidia.com/dgx/dgx-station-development-guide/porting/software-requirements.html). Allow outbound access to the container registry, Hugging Face, and package repositories.
*   At least 464 GB of free disk space on each Station for its copy of the checkpoint, plus room for the vLLM container image and temporary files.
*   Acceptance of the NVIDIA Open Model Agreement and the original GLM-5.3 license terms, listed on the [model card](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/GLM-5.3-NVFP4#licenseterms-of-use). SPEED-Bench is governed by the [NVIDIA Evaluation Dataset License Agreement](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/SPEED-Bench/blob/main/License.pdf).
*   A Hugging Face account and read access token, with access to the gated [cais/hle](https://huggingface.co/datasets/cais/hle) dataset: sign in, open its page, and select **Agree and access repository**. Step 5 downloads SPEED-Bench prompts from this dataset.

The companion video follows the same workflow.

_Video 1. Walkthrough of preparation, inference, benchmarking, and shutdown_

## Step 1. Prepare the two Stations

This tutorial uses a separate computer, such as your laptop, to manage both Stations. Start by opening an SSH session to each Station from that computer. Alternatively, work from a local terminal on each Station. Run every command in this step on both Stations unless it starts with “On A.”

The two Stations run the same container and checkpoint in different roles: Station A (rank 0) hosts the API, and Station B (rank 1) runs only a worker, with no API server.

First, check Docker access and collect the network values you’ll use later:

`docker version`

`ibdev2netdev`

`ip -br addr`

| **Note:** If the `docker version` output has no `Server` section, the client cannot reach the Docker daemon. If the error is `permission denied`, follow the [Docker post-installation procedure](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/linux-postinstall/): add your user to the `docker` group with `sudo usermod -aG docker "$USER"`, run `exit`, then reconnect and rerun `docker version`. The `docker` group grants root-level privileges. |
| --- |

The `ibdev2netdev` output lists the two direct rails, `cx8r0` and `cx8r1`. Pick one for serving traffic, for example `cx8r1`, and note two things for it on each Station:

*   **Its RDMA device**, on the `ibdev2netdev` line that ends with the rail’s name. In `mlx5_1 port 1 ==> cx8r1 (Up)`, the device is `mlx5_1`.
*   **Its IPv4 address**, on the `ip -br addr` line that starts with the rail’s name. In `cx8r1 UP 192.168.101.1/24`, the address is `192.168.101.1`.

The rail name and device are the same on both Stations; only the IPv4 address differs.

Next, create `~/glm53.env` on each Station. This file stores the values that later commands use:

```
nano ~/glm53.env
```

Paste the following block and replace each `<...>` placeholder, keeping the quotes, with the values you noted.

`RANK=``"<NODE_RANK>"`

`HEAD_IP=``"<STATION_A_IPV4_ADDRESS>"`

`WORKER_IP=``"<STATION_B_IPV4_ADDRESS>"`

`RAIL_IFACE=``"<RAIL_NAME>"`

`RAIL_HCA=``"<RDMA_DEVICE>"`

`IMG=vllm``/vllm-openai``:v0.30.0-aarch64`

`IMG+=@sha256:4864d46625cbc3307623e29ac742030655e27249feba7b97ec925ce4cc4dfb56`

`MODEL_REPO=nvidia``/GLM-5``.3-NVFP4`

`MODEL_REV=e3b8f9f2fad29727dfa95e766c5cac18ea1414bf`

`MODEL_HOST=``"$HOME/models/GLM-5.3-NVFP4"`

`CONTAINER=glm53-full`

`PORT=8000`

`if``[``"$RANK"``= 0 ];``then`

```NODE_IP=$HEAD_IP; PEER_IP=$WORKER_IP`

`else`

```NODE_IP=$WORKER_IP; PEER_IP=$HEAD_IP`

`fi`

`GPU_UUID=$(nvidia-smi --query-gpu=uuid,name --``format``=csv,noheader |`

```awk``-F,``'$2 ~ /GB300/ {gsub(/ /,"",$1); print $1; exit}'``)`

For example, with the default addresses on `cx8r1`, Station A’s file starts like this. Station B’s file is identical except for `RANK="1"`:

```
RANK="0"
HEAD_IP="192.168.101.1"
WORKER_IP="192.168.101.2"
RAIL_IFACE="cx8r1"
RAIL_HCA="mlx5_1"
```

`MODEL_HOST` is built from your home directory, and Step 2 copies the checkpoint over SSH to the same path on Station B.

| **Note:** Later steps start with `source ~/glm53.env` to load these values. **Run this command again whenever you open a new SSH session.** |
| --- |

On both Stations, load the values and check storage, connectivity, and baseline memory:

```
source ~/glm53.env
mkdir -p "$MODEL_HOST" && df -h "$MODEL_HOST"
ethtool "$RAIL_IFACE"
ip link show dev "$RAIL_IFACE"
ping -I "$RAIL_IFACE" -M do -s 8972 -c 3 "$PEER_IP"
timedatectl show -p NTPSynchronized --value
nvidia-smi
```

These checks catch cabling and addressing mistakes before they surface as NCCL timeouts. Expect a `400000Mb/s` link, MTU 9000, successful jumbo-frame pings, and synchronized time. `nvidia-smi` should show no compute processes on the GB300. On a Station with a display GPU, Xorg can appear on both GPUs with a few MiB.

| **Tip:** Note the GPU memory use shown by `nvidia-smi`; Step 4 compares it with the loaded model. |
| --- |

Step 2 copies the checkpoint from A to B over SSH, so A needs passwordless access to B. On A, create a key without a passphrase (see [SSH keys](https://ubuntu.com/server/docs/how-to/security/openssh-server/#ssh-keys) for details), copy its public key to B after checking B’s host fingerprint, and confirm the login:

```
ssh-keygen -t ed25519
ssh-copy-id "$WORKER_IP"
ssh -o BatchMode=yes "$WORKER_IP" hostname
```

## Step 2. Download and copy the model

Tensor parallelism requires both ranks to run the same software against the same weights. Start by pulling the pinned image on both Stations:

```
docker pull "$IMG" &&
docker image inspect "$IMG" --format '{{.Architecture}} {{.RepoDigests}}'
```

The pull can take several minutes. Matching arm64 digests mean both ranks run identical software.

On A, download the pinned checkpoint. At about 464 GB, it takes roughly an hour at 1 Gb/s, or about six minutes at 10 Gb/s:

```
mkdir -p "$MODEL_HOST"
docker run --rm --network host -v "$MODEL_HOST:/model" \
  --entrypoint bash "$IMG" -lc \
  "exec hf download '$MODEL_REPO' --revision '$MODEL_REV' --local-dir /model"
```

When `hf download` prints `Downloaded`, copy the files to B. On A:

```
ssh "$WORKER_IP" "mkdir -p '$MODEL_HOST'" &&
rsync -aH --info=progress2 --exclude '.cache/' \
  "$MODEL_HOST/" "$WORKER_IP:$MODEL_HOST/"
```

Each disk keeps the full checkpoint; vLLM partitions the weights across the GPUs at load time, with no further quantization.

On A, compare both copies (the check reads B’s file list over SSH), then validate the checkpoint:

```
(
  set -euo pipefail
  L=$(find "$MODEL_HOST" -path '*/.cache' -prune -o \
    -type f -printf '%P %s\n' | LC_ALL=C sort | sha256sum)
  R=$(ssh "$WORKER_IP" "set -o pipefail; find '$MODEL_HOST' \
    -path '*/.cache' -prune -o -type f -printf '%P %s\\n' | \
    LC_ALL=C sort | sha256sum")
  test "$L" = "$R"
  test "$(find "$MODEL_HOST" -maxdepth 1 \
    -name 'model-*-of-00050.safetensors' | wc -l)" = 50
  python3 -c "import json; c=json.load(open('$MODEL_HOST/config.json')); \
assert c['architectures']==['GlmMoeDsaForCausalLM']; \
assert c['quantization_config']['quant_algo']=='MIXED_PRECISION'"
  echo MODEL_READY
)
```

`MODEL_READY` means both Stations hold the same file names and sizes in the expected layout. `MIXED_PRECISION` is expected: NVFP4 quantization targets MoE-block linear weights and activations, not every tensor.

## Step 3. Launch the distributed service

This step turns two machines into one service: the same launch script runs on both Stations, reads `~/glm53.env`, and starts one vLLM rank on each. Two settings matter most if you adapt it: `--max-model-len 98304`, the context ceiling in tokens, which covers input plus output, and `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.93`, which gives vLLM 93% of GPU memory. If you change other flags, change one at a time and test again.

For the latest recommended configurations, see [NVIDIA’s Local AI recipe repository](https://nvidia.github.io/local-ai-inference-recipes/hardware/dgx-station-2gpu/index.html).

| **Security note:**`--host 0.0.0.0` with `--network host` exposes the unauthenticated API on every Station A interface, including management. Firewall the port to intended clients, and add authentication and TLS before wider access. |
| --- |

On both Stations, create a file named `~/launch-glm53.sh`:

```
nano ~/launch-glm53.sh
```

The script enables multi-token prediction (MTP), a form of speculative decoding: the model’s MTP layer drafts four tokens per step, and vLLM verifies them with the full model before accepting them, so each step can produce several tokens. The gain depends on how often drafts are accepted, which varies with the prompt.

FP8 KV-cache storage halves cache memory compared with 16-bit storage, leaving room for more tokens. Prefix caching is enabled to avoid reprocessing prompt prefixes the server has already seen. Paste the script below; it checks your configuration, finds the RoCE GID index for the selected rail, and starts this Station’s vLLM rank in a container:

`set``-euo pipefail`

`source``"$HOME/glm53.env"`

`case``"$RANK"``in``0|1) ;; *)``echo``"Invalid RANK"``>&2;``exit``1;;``esac`

`test``-n``"$GPU_UUID"`

`test``-f``"$MODEL_HOST/config.json"`

`GID_INDEX=$(``/usr/sbin/show_gids``2>``/dev/null``|`

```awk``-``v``d=``"$RAIL_HCA"``-``v``ip=``"$NODE_IP"``\`

```'$1==d && $5==ip && $6=="v2" {g=$3} END {if(g!="") print g}'``)`

`test``-n``"$GID_INDEX"`

`HEADLESS=`

`if``[``"$RANK"``= 1 ];``then``HEADLESS=--headless;``fi`

`SPEC_CONFIG=``'{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":4}'`

`KERNEL_CONFIG=``'{"enable_flashinfer_autotune":false,"moe_backend":"flashinfer_cutlass"}'`

Title: Anthropic CEO Amodei admits "there's a huge uncertainty in what's going to happen next year" days before a record IPO

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-ceo-amodei-admits-theres-a-huge-uncertainty-in-whats-going-to-happen-next-year-days-before-a-record-ipo/

Published Time: 2026-11-14T19:05:17+00:00

Markdown Content:
**Days before what could be the largest IPO in history, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei names the central weakness of his business model. Nobody knows how the company's compute investments will pay off, he says. It isn't the first time he's sounded this warning.**

"There's a huge uncertainty in what's going to happen next year." Speaking at a JPMorgan Chase investor event in New York on Friday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei used that line to sum up the problem facing his company.

The admission came, of all times, in the last days before the company's planned Nov. 19 IPO, and compute was one of several topics in the conversation. [Speaking with JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon](https://x.com/firesidealpha/status/2121303747012030844), he said, "Compute is the deepest business dilemma that the company faces."

AI technology is advancing so fast that, Amodei said, no one yet knows how that progress will translate into economic value. But compute has to be bought one to two years ahead, before anyone knows whether revenue will justify the cost.

If Anthropic buys too little, he said, it won't have the resources for customers and new technologies, and revenue takes a hit. Buying too much carries the opposite risk. "You can financially overextend yourself," Amodei said.

## $901 billion bet on an uncertain future

Anthropic has already committed nearly $901 billion, most of it to compute and chips, [according to Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-13/anthropic-ceo-calls-computing-power-deepest-business-dilemma). Roughly $71 billion of that comes due by September 2027. Bloomberg notes that figure exceeds the market cap of about two-thirds of S&P 500 companies.

Back in February 2026, Amodei [warned in much sharper terms](https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-ceo-dario-amodei-suggests-openai-doesnt-really-understand-the-risks-theyre-taking/) that he could buy $1 trillion of compute starting at the end of 2027 and go bankrupt if revenue fell short. Being off by just one year could mean bankruptcy. He is not sure some competitors have done the math, and he said they don't really understand the risks they're taking. The stakes have kept rising since then.

## Anthropic wants the IPO to cushion against the unknown

Amodei described two ways Anthropic softens the compute dilemma: gross margins and cash on the balance sheet. He said the company’s gross margins are "quite good," especially compared with other players, and that Anthropic has a large cash balance and is seeking to raise more.

The company also buys relatively little compute upfront, then can turn to the spot market for additional capacity if business goes better than expected. Amodei compared that approach to buying insurance, saying it leaves Anthropic covered if results fall short while allowing it to invest more when things go well.

The compute bets were the biggest reason to go public: the more cash Anthropic holds, he said, the wider its margin for error between a world with too little compute and one with too much.

Anthropic plans to raise up to $64.4 billion through the IPO and another $26 billion through a private placement, Bloomberg reports. Combined, that would make it the largest IPO ever. The offering is reportedly already about [six times oversubscribed](https://the-decoder.com/anthropics-ipo-is-six-times-oversubscribed-and-on-track-to-become-the-largest-public-offering-in-history/).

Anthropic's annualized revenue run rate hit [$81 billion](https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-opens-its-books-for-wall-street-showing-record-revenue-and-mounting-obligations/) at the end of October, up $10 billion from late September, according to company filings. Bloomberg says the rising popularity of AI products, including its coding models, has helped fuel revenue growth.

Amodei struck a relaxed tone about the IPO's timing, saying he wasn't fixated on a specific month or particular market conditions. Anthropic, he noted, grew from nothing to its current size in just six years. The most common advice he got before the IPO, or the advice that resonated most, he said, was something like "never let your company be worth a single dollar more than it's really worth." That, he said, is very similar to a model Anthropic uses internally: "under-promise and over-deliver."

In the same conversation, though, Amodei said he hopes AI will cure cancer and Alzheimer's within five to 15 years, adding that he doesn't know exactly. In Silicon Valley, that may already count as under-promising.

articles.content:
agweb
A browser for coding agents on macOS, built on WebKit (Safari's engine). I run several coding agents at once, and Playwright's Chrome windows kept stealing my keyboard, while headless browsers got blocked by some sites and left me guessing what went wrong. agweb is one window that never takes focus: agents drive it from the shell with
agweb
, a playwright-cli-style command, and you watch them all live.
Idle tabs are suspended: on my Mac five open pages sit at 0% CPU, where Chrome's GPU process kept five to seven cores busy.
Five idle pages
Memory
agweb
590 MB
Headless Chrome
730 MB
Playwright Chrome
1.6 GB
Never steals focus.
No window comes to the front, nothing pops up. Dialogs, changing tabs, file pickers and downloads are answered in code.
You can always see it.
The dashboard (⌘D) shows every tab of every agent at once, live, with each agent's last command. And it is always a real window: some sites block headless browsers, and headless leaves you guessing what went wrong.
Many agents at once.
Each agent works in its own workspace with its own tabs, grouped by agent in the sidebar.
Log in once.
A named profile (
-p work
) keeps its logins and is shared by every agent using it, at the same time.
Light.
Idle tabs are throttled and then suspended, so open pages cost almost nothing once nobody uses them.
Acts like a person.
Clicks and keys are native macOS events, and the pointer moves like a hand, so hover menus and drag-and-drop work.
Made for agents.
Snapshots give each element a ref that lasts while it is on the page.
snapshot --diff
and
find
show only what matters, and every action reports what it changed.
Passwords stay out of the transcript.
fill --secret-cmd 'pass show site'
types a secret the agent never sees in replies. 1Password and Bitwarden CLIs work too.
No ads.
Ads and trackers are blocked with uBlock Origin's lists, which agweb downloads every 4 days. An agent testing analytics can turn it off for its own workspace (
agweb -w task adblock off
).
Demo videos.
video-start
records a tab to MP4, with the pointer and clicks drawn in.
Install
Needs macOS 26 or later. Download
Agweb.dmg
from
Releases
, drag Agweb to Applications and open it. Then:
Help ▸ Install Command Line Tool
Help ▸ Install Agent Skill (for Claude Code and Codex).
Both are links into the app, so they update with it.
To build from source instead (Xcode 26 or later):
./scripts/build.sh
build/Agweb.app/Contents/Helpers/agweb install-cli
agweb install-skill
Use
agweb -w task open en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebKit
#
a workspace for this task; starts the app if needed
agweb -w task snapshot
#
the page as a tree with [ref=eN] handles
agweb -w task click
'
role=button[name="Main menu"]
'
The click's reply already says what it did, so the agent needs no second snapshot:
### Changes
  - navigation "Site" [ref=e2]
-   - button "Main menu" [ref=e3]
+   - button "Main menu" [checked] [expanded] [ref=e3]
+   - list [ref=e1167]
+     - listitem [ref=e1168]
+       - link "Main page" [ref=e1169]
agweb help
lists every command. Settings (⌘,) has text size, dashboard columns, a CPU and memory readout and the ad blocker switch.
Compared with playwright-cli
Same commands where possible, so agents already know them; a Playwright name it lacks suggests its own (
scroll-to
→
scroll-into-view
). On top:
Replies say what changed
: fetches started, lines added or removed, dialogs, popups, downloads, console errors. No snapshot after every step, so far fewer tokens.
Refs last
while the element is on the page.
ask
hands the tab to you for a login, MFA code or CAPTCHA, without taking focus.
Actions wait
for the fetches they caused, so agents rarely sleep.
text
returns the page's article as markdown.
Shared logins
: agents on one profile run at once; a Chrome profile opens in one browser only.
Limits
WebKit only: no Chrome DevTools Protocol, so Playwright and Chrome extensions can't attach, and Chrome-only sites may misbehave.
route
mocks fetch and XHR only;
requests
lists images, scripts and styles by URL only (
--static
).
The ad blocker can't run uBlock's scripts, so YouTube ads and some "turn off your ad blocker" walls get through.
For what it can't do, use Playwright.
Develop
./scripts/selftest.sh
runs every command against a local page in a separate instance;
swift test
runs the unit tests.
AGWEB_ROOT=/tmp/dir
starts a second instance beside your own that keeps everything in that folder.
Defuddle
(MIT) is bundled for
text
.
